question: 128. Deputy Darren O'Rourke asked the Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science to provide an update on plans to deliver new, permanent accommodation for a school (details supplied); and if he will make a statement on the matter. [5367/26]
answer: Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science (Deputy James Lawless) Louth Meath ETB’s FET College Major Capital project proposal involves the construction of a new, fit-for-purpose facility on a greenfield site. This new facility is intended to replace the current rented accommodation in Dunboyne and is one of twelve projects currently being advanced under this programme. LMETB’s preliminary business case for the proposed infrastructure they wish to deliver in Dunboyne is currently at evaluation stage. This evaluation cannot be finalised until such time the site has been secured, as the acquisition of a suitable site that can support the required infrastructure is a key determine when assessing a business case. LMETB have identified a preferred site option and are continuing to progress work on this acquisition with relevant legal and site due diligence ongoing. The progression of proposals under the FET College Major Capital Programme is a key priority for my department. My department officials recently met with all 12 of the Chief Executives who have projects under this programme. At this meeting ETBs were informed that they need to prioritise the appointment of design teams for these projects in 2026 for those that are ready to do so. Supporting learners and educators across all regions including across the Louth Meath ETB region remains a top priority for my department, and I remain committed to ensuring there is appropriate infrastructure in place to meet their needs.

question: 154. Deputy Cathy Bennett asked the Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science his plans to ensure adequate provision of accommodation for students. [6990/26]
answer: Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science (Deputy James Lawless) I am taking decisive action to increase the supply of student accommodation across Ireland so that students can have access to high-quality housing close to their campuses. A central part of this is the Technological Sector Student Accommodation Programme (TSSAP), which will be extended to traditional universities. Through this programme, I am supporting the delivery of Purpose-Built Student Accommodation (PBSA) on or near campuses, particularly in areas where provision has historically been limited. Rent-a-Room accommodation is another important source of student beds and will be actively promoted through the Strategy. These developments will be evidence-based, regionally targeted, and designed to meet growing demand while reducing reliance on long daily commutes. Students facing daily journeys of over three hours are considered to require on-campus or nearby accommodation, and addressing this need is a key objective in the strategy. I will facilitate the development of sites on HEI-owned land and support collaboration with the private sector. In addition, the reduction of VAT from 13.5% to 9% on new apartments, combined with the adoption of standardised design models and modern construction methods, improves project viability, reduces development costs, and enables accommodation to be delivered efficiently at scale. Through these measures, I am addressing the need for access to safe, modern, and sustainable accommodation that meets the needs of Ireland’s growing higher education sector.

question: 204. Deputy Erin McGreehan asked the Minister for Transport the extent to which his Department monitors working conditions, pay and accommodation for non-EU crew members on Irish-registered vessels operating in inshore fisheries; the way in which this monitoring is coordinated with the Department of Enterprise, Tourism and Employment and the Workplace Relations Commission; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [7327/26]
answer: Minister of State at the Department of Transport Under the relevant legislation (the European Union (International Labour Organisation Work in Fishing Convention) (Crew List and Fisherman's Work Agreement) Regulations 2020 - S.I. 333 of 2020), the Marine Survey Office (MSO), a division of the Department, is designated as the competent authority in the State for the purposes of these Regulations. The MSO monitors the hours of work and rest and standards of accommodation of all fishers working on board vessels of 15m length overall (LOA) and above, and of 'share fishers' working alongside those working under contract. When inspecting working conditions on board fishing vessels the MSO makes no distinction between conditions for EU and non-EU fishers and applies the same standards of treatment to all on board. Issues relating to pay are monitored by the Workplace Relations Commission (WRC), while the Department of Enterprise, Tourism and Employment is responsible for issuing the relevant work permits to non-EU fishers. Inspections by these organisations focus on different requirements and their inspection regimes are carried out on a separate legal basis.

question: 330. Deputy Martin Daly asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration whether the accommodation recognition payment for hosts providing accommodation to beneficiaries of temporary protection will be extended beyond its current end date of 31 March 2026; when a decision on the future of the scheme will be made; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [7135/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration The Accommodation Recognition Payment (ARP) was introduced to recognise the generosity of people who have opened their homes to provide accommodation to temporary protection beneficiaries from Ukraine. The scheme is provided for in Part 2 of the Civil Law (Miscellaneous Provisions) Act 2022 and is administered by the Department of Social Protection on my behalf.The scheme has been successful in accommodating some 63,000 temporary protection beneficiaries outside of State-contracted accommodation since it commenced in 2022. Some 42,000 people are currently living in almost 23,500 hosted accommodations with the support of the scheme.The ARP scheme is currently in place until 31 March 2026 but may be extended by Ministerial order in accordance with the governing legislation. It is my intention to seek Oireachtas approval to extend the scheme for a further year to 31 March 2027 to align with the timeframe for the Temporary Protection Directive and to allow for an orderly wind-down of the scheme in advance of the end of the application of that EU Directive to the war in Ukraine.Section 4(2) of the Act of 2022 enables me to make such a change, following consultation with the Minister for Social Protection and the Minister for Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation. I can confirm that I have commenced those consultations.The Act of 2022 also requires, where such an order is proposed to be made, that a draft of the order be laid before each House of the Oireachtas and that the order shall not be made until a resolution approving the draft has been passed by each House of the Oireachtas. I intend to complete the required statutory processes before the current scheme termination date of 31 March.

question: 331. Deputy Donna McGettigan asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number of Gardaí stationed in Newmarket on Fergus, County Clare; the number on sick leave; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [7016/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration In the interest of transparency, An Garda Síochána publish information in relation to the number of available members by Division and Station which is publicly available and can be found at the following link: www.garda.ie/garda/en/about-us/our-departments/human-resources-and-people-development/garda-hr-directorate/garda-strength-breakdown-2025/garda-strength-breakdown-2025.html The Deputy should select the file titled “Garda Members by Division District Station 2009 to latest date ” for a breakdown of available members of An Garda Síochána in the Clare/Tipperary Division and in stations in Co Clare. The Garda Commissioner is responsible for the management and administration of Garda business under Section 33 of the Policing, Security and Community Safety Act 2024. This includes the management of sick leave for Garda personnel and all other internal Garda HR matters. As Minister, I have no role in these independent functions. It is not possible to confirm the sick leave status of individual members for data protection reasons. It should be noted that An Garda Síochána do not police on a station basis, but rather on a Divisional basis and see stations as locations within communities for people to attend, and for resources to be accommodated. Policing for an area will be delivered using all resources in a Community Engagement Area and supported by Divisional resources and units. While the Garda Commissioner is operationally responsible for the allocation of Garda resources, I regularly engage with him to ensure An Garda Síochána have the resources they need to deliver an effective police service.

question: 333. Deputy Carol Nolan asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the projected impact of the International Protection Bill 2026 on reducing the overall number of asylum applications processed annually in the State, particularly through the introduction of stricter admissibility checks and accelerated procedures; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [7112/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 333, 335, 336, 339 and 341 together. My Department continues to focus on preparing for the EU Migration and Asylum Pact in advance of June 2026. The Pact will provide a fair, sustainable and efficient asylum procedure. This will be achieved through convergence in asylum practices across the EU. The new International Protection Bill 2026 gives effect to the measures of the EU Migration and Asylum Pact. Enactment of the Bill and commencement of the Act is required by 12 June 2026. The International Protection Bill 2026 delivers on the Programme for Government commitment to implement the new EU Migration and Asylum Pact by 12 June 2026. This Bill represents the most significant reform of Irish asylum laws in the history of the State. It will put in place a new framework to manage migration and asylum for the long term. It will improve decision-making structures within the international protection system and provide faster timelines for the processing of international protection applications. The overall objective of the Bill is to provide a fair, sustainable and efficient asylum procedure. The Bill provides for the timeframes for the different procedures under which an international protection application can be examined, in accordance with the 2024 Asylum Procedure Regulation and the 2024 Asylum and Migration Management Regulation (AMMR). These timeframes are 6 months for standard procedures, 3 months for the accelerated procedure, 2 months for the admissibility procedure, and in procedures for determining the Member State responsible in accordance with the AMMR, 6 months. The Asylum Border Procedure has a 12-week time limit for first instance and appeal decisions to be completed for applicants from countries of origin with a recognition rate of 20% or less across the EU, or for those who intentionally mislead the authorities by presenting false information or documents or by withholding relevant information or documents, or are deemed a security risk. The Bill designates the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration as the determining authority for the purposes of the Pact measures. Examinations to determine whether a person qualifies as a refugee or is eligible for subsidiary protection will be conducted by the determining authority and the new appeals body, the Tribunal for Asylum and Returns Appeals (TARA), which will replace the International Protection Appeals Tribunal (IPAT). Officers of the Minister will directly make decisions on international protection applications, including return decisions, which may be appealed to TARA, which may issue a fresh decision that is declaratory in nature. A negative decision will be issued as one decision, which will include: (i) a decision that the applicant does not qualify for refugee status; (ii) a decision that the applicant is not eligible for subsidiary protection; and (iii) a return decision. The Bill, therefore, for the first time in Irish legislation, provides that a return decision (which will be similar in effect to a deportation order) will be issued together with a decision rejecting an international protection application. These decisions will be subject to simultaneous appeal to TARA. This faster decision-making means that successful applicants will be granted international protection sooner, and those whose applications are refused can be returned to their country of origin sooner. In relation to processing costs to the State, it will be settled annually in the course of engagement on the Estimates process, as is currently the case. In the medium to long-term this investment will show a return in the form of decreasing annual costs because of the improved, faster processing it will enable, thereby reducing the time an applicant remains in the system, and reducing significant accommodation and other costs. I would also note that there is a substantial EU budget to be distributed through the Asylum, Migration and Integration Fund (AMIF) being made available to support implementation of the Pact across the EU. Ireland has received approximately €21.5m under the AMIF Thematic Facility Specific Action and a further approximately €8.9m AMIF funding will be made available on foot of a mid-term review. On accommodation more widely, my Department is already working to move away from commercial provision to more State-owned accommodation. While commissioning emergency commercial accommodation will continue to be necessary in the short to medium term, it is being contracted on a short-term basis, which enables the State to decommission this capacity with agility as contracts expire or demand fluctuates. It is hoped that the creation of a core supply of State-owned accommodation, of both emergency and permanent options, will also allow more strategic direction accommodation types, location and dispersal patterns nationwide. These reforms will help to drive down costs and to curtail the growth seen over recent years in the accommodation system. Managing the return of persons who no longer have a right to stay in the State is an integral part of a functioning immigration system and will be done with full respect for human rights and the principle of non-refoulement. The International Protection Bill provides that applicants for international protection who are refused international protection and no longer have a right to remain in the State, will be issued a return decision and required to leave the State.

question: 334. Deputy Carol Nolan asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration if he will outline the criteria for designating additional safe countries of origin under the International Protection Bill 2026 to further limit ineligible claims and expedite returns; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [7113/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 334 and 338 together. I am fully committed to ensuring that Ireland’s International Protection system is robust, and rules based, and that our borders are protected. The International Protection Bill 2026 delivers on the Programme for Government commitment to implement the new EU Migration and Asylum Pact by 12 June 2026. This Bill represents the most significant reform of Irish asylum laws in the history of the State. It will put in place a new framework to manage migration and asylum for the long term. It will improve decision-making structures within the international protection system and provide faster timelines for the processing of international protection applications. The overall objective of the Bill is to provide a fair, sustainable and efficient asylum procedure that is consistent with how asylum laws operate across the EU. I can inform the Deputy that under section 215 of the International Protection Bill 2026, the Minister for Justice will be empowered to make an order designating a country as a safe country of origin. A country may only be designated as a safe country of origin only if I am satisfied that, on the basis of the legal situation, the application of the law within a democratic system and the general political circumstances, it can be shown that there is no persecution and no real risk of serious harm. Ireland currently has fifteen countries designated as safe countries of origin: Albania, Bosnia and Herzegovina, North Macedonia, Georgia, Montenegro, Kosovo, Serbia, South Africa, Botswana, Algeria, Brazil, Egypt, India, Malawi and Morocco. I will continue to keep the list of safe countries under review. The Asylum Procedures Regulation (Regulation 2024/1348) makes provision for the designation of safe countries of origin at European Union level, and pursuant to its provisions the European Commission has now proposed such a list. Common designation of safe countries of origin at Union level should ensure that the safe country of origin concept is applied by all Member States in a uniform manner in relation to applicants whose countries of origin are designated as safe at Union level. The proposal, which Ireland has supported, is now at an advanced stage in the EU legislative process. It provides that all candidate countries for the EU would be designated as safe countries of origin, along with certain other countries that have been proposed based on information from relevant organisations. A backstop provision will ensure that Ukraine, an EU candidate country, is not considered a safe country of origin while the ongoing conflict continues. The overall effect of the proposal would be to add Moldova, Türkiye, Bangladesh, Colombia and Tunisia to the countries already recognised by Ireland as safe third countries at national level. The Proposal does not propose to amend Article 64 of the Asylum Procedure Regulation, therefore, the right of Member States to designate additional countries outside the common list will continue. One of the new provisions in the EU Pact is the Asylum Border Procedure. This will provide for a twelve-week timeframe, extendable to sixteen weeks in certain circumstances, for the examination of applications for international protection, including the appeal to the new Tribunal for Asylum Returns and Appeals. The asylum border procedure will apply to applicants from countries of origin with a recognition rate of 20% or less across the EU, applicants who have intentionally misled the authorities by presenting false information or documents or by withholding relevant information or documents, applicants who have, in bad faith, destroyed or disposed of documents in order to prevent the establishment of their identity or nationality, or applicants who are deemed a national security risk. The aim is to issue decisions in the quickest time possible to those less likely to have an entitlement to international protection. In accordance with the Asylum Procedures Regulation, I am providing for this procedure in the International Protection Bill 2026 which is currently before the Oireachtas.

question: 337. Deputy Carol Nolan asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the way in which the three-year bar on family reunification applications for newly recognised refugees under the International Protection Bill 2026, along with requirements for financial self-sufficiency, will contribute to controlling secondary migration flows into the State; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [7116/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration Migration plays an important role in Ireland's economic, social, and community life, and for those granted international protection, the ability to reunite with close family members can be a significant factor in supporting stability and integration. At the same time, family reunification policy must operate within the context of finite public resources, the State's responsibility to manage migration in the interests of the economic and social wellbeing of the country, and the importance of encouraging independence and self-sufficiency from an integration perspective. I will introduce family reunification provisions into the International Protection Bill at Committee Stage that reflect those aims and that will more closely align with other EU Member States. An important consideration in all family reunification applications is the ability of the sponsor to demonstrate a clear capacity to provide for their family members if they are to be granted a permission to come to Ireland. I also propose to include a provision that adults who are beneficiaries of international protection will not be entitled to seek family reunification for a certain period following their grant of international protection. These new measures contribute to managing migration flows by ensuring that family reunification is exercised within a structured and proportionate framework that is broadly consistent with other EU Member States. This consistency can play a role in supporting the orderly management of migration while continuing to support family reunification where integration and self-sufficiency have been established. This approach reflects the Government's objective of promoting effective integration outcomes for both sponsors and their family members. In that context, my Department invests in a range of measures related to integration, including community led initiatives, to support the inclusion of migrants and their families in Irish society.

Ireland currently has fifteen countries designated as safe countries of origin: Albania, Bosnia and Herzegovina, North Macedonia, Georgia, Montenegro, Kosovo, Serbia, South Africa, Botswana, Algeria, Brazil, Egypt, India, Malawi and Morocco. I will continue to keep the list of safe countries under review. The Asylum Procedures Regulation (Regulation 2024/1348) makes provision for the designation of safe countries of origin at European Union level, and pursuant to its provisions the European Commission has now proposed such a list. Common designation of safe countries of origin at Union level should ensure that the safe country of origin concept is applied by all Member States in a uniform manner in relation to applicants whose countries of origin are designated as safe at Union level. The proposal, which Ireland has supported, is now at an advanced stage in the EU legislative process. It provides that all candidate countries for the EU would be designated as safe countries of origin, along with certain other countries that have been proposed based on information from relevant organisations. A backstop provision will ensure that Ukraine, an EU candidate country, is not considered a safe country of origin while the ongoing conflict continues. The overall effect of the proposal would be to add Moldova, Türkiye, Bangladesh, Colombia and Tunisia to the countries already recognised by Ireland as safe third countries at national level. The Proposal does not propose to amend Article 64 of the Asylum Procedure Regulation, therefore, the right of Member States to designate additional countries outside the common list will continue. One of the new provisions in the EU Pact is the Asylum Border Procedure. This will provide for a twelve-week timeframe, extendable to sixteen weeks in certain circumstances, for the examination of applications for international protection, including the appeal to the new Tribunal for Asylum Returns and Appeals. The asylum border procedure will apply to applicants from countries of origin with a recognition rate of 20% or less across the EU, applicants who have intentionally misled the authorities by presenting false information or documents or by withholding relevant information or documents, applicants who have, in bad faith, destroyed or disposed of documents in order to prevent the establishment of their identity or nationality, or applicants who are deemed a national security risk. The aim is to issue decisions in the quickest time possible to those less likely to have an entitlement to international protection. In accordance with the Asylum Procedures Regulation, I am providing for this procedure in the International Protection Bill 2026 which is currently before the Oireachtas.

question: 339. Deputy Carol Nolan asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the projected reduction in accommodation demands for international protection applicants as a result of the faster decision-making processes and increased returns outlined in the International Protection Bill 2026; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [7118/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 333, 335, 336, 339 and 341 together. My Department continues to focus on preparing for the EU Migration and Asylum Pact in advance of June 2026. The Pact will provide a fair, sustainable and efficient asylum procedure. This will be achieved through convergence in asylum practices across the EU. The new International Protection Bill 2026 gives effect to the measures of the EU Migration and Asylum Pact. Enactment of the Bill and commencement of the Act is required by 12 June 2026. The International Protection Bill 2026 delivers on the Programme for Government commitment to implement the new EU Migration and Asylum Pact by 12 June 2026. This Bill represents the most significant reform of Irish asylum laws in the history of the State. It will put in place a new framework to manage migration and asylum for the long term. It will improve decision-making structures within the international protection system and provide faster timelines for the processing of international protection applications. The overall objective of the Bill is to provide a fair, sustainable and efficient asylum procedure. The Bill provides for the timeframes for the different procedures under which an international protection application can be examined, in accordance with the 2024 Asylum Procedure Regulation and the 2024 Asylum and Migration Management Regulation (AMMR). These timeframes are 6 months for standard procedures, 3 months for the accelerated procedure, 2 months for the admissibility procedure, and in procedures for determining the Member State responsible in accordance with the AMMR, 6 months. The Asylum Border Procedure has a 12-week time limit for first instance and appeal decisions to be completed for applicants from countries of origin with a recognition rate of 20% or less across the EU, or for those who intentionally mislead the authorities by presenting false information or documents or by withholding relevant information or documents, or are deemed a security risk. The Bill designates the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration as the determining authority for the purposes of the Pact measures. Examinations to determine whether a person qualifies as a refugee or is eligible for subsidiary protection will be conducted by the determining authority and the new appeals body, the Tribunal for Asylum and Returns Appeals (TARA), which will replace the International Protection Appeals Tribunal (IPAT). Officers of the Minister will directly make decisions on international protection applications, including return decisions, which may be appealed to TARA, which may issue a fresh decision that is declaratory in nature. A negative decision will be issued as one decision, which will include: (i) a decision that the applicant does not qualify for refugee status; (ii) a decision that the applicant is not eligible for subsidiary protection; and (iii) a return decision. The Bill, therefore, for the first time in Irish legislation, provides that a return decision (which will be similar in effect to a deportation order) will be issued together with a decision rejecting an international protection application. These decisions will be subject to simultaneous appeal to TARA. This faster decision-making means that successful applicants will be granted international protection sooner, and those whose applications are refused can be returned to their country of origin sooner. In relation to processing costs to the State, it will be settled annually in the course of engagement on the Estimates process, as is currently the case. In the medium to long-term this investment will show a return in the form of decreasing annual costs because of the improved, faster processing it will enable, thereby reducing the time an applicant remains in the system, and reducing significant accommodation and other costs. I would also note that there is a substantial EU budget to be distributed through the Asylum, Migration and Integration Fund (AMIF) being made available to support implementation of the Pact across the EU. Ireland has received approximately €21.5m under the AMIF Thematic Facility Specific Action and a further approximately €8.9m AMIF funding will be made available on foot of a mid-term review. On accommodation more widely, my Department is already working to move away from commercial provision to more State-owned accommodation. While commissioning emergency commercial accommodation will continue to be necessary in the short to medium term, it is being contracted on a short-term basis, which enables the State to decommission this capacity with agility as contracts expire or demand fluctuates. It is hoped that the creation of a core supply of State-owned accommodation, of both emergency and permanent options, will also allow more strategic direction accommodation types, location and dispersal patterns nationwide. These reforms will help to drive down costs and to curtail the growth seen over recent years in the accommodation system. Managing the return of persons who no longer have a right to stay in the State is an integral part of a functioning immigration system and will be done with full respect for human rights and the principle of non-refoulement. The International Protection Bill provides that applicants for international protection who are refused international protection and no longer have a right to remain in the State, will be issued a return decision and required to leave the State.

question: 340. Deputy Carol Nolan asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration if he intends to expand the list of accelerated processing categories under the International Protection Bill 2026 to include more nationalities with historically low recognition rates, thereby limiting prolonged stays in the State; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [7119/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I am fully committed to ensuring that Ireland’s International Protection system is robust, and rules based, and that our borders are protected. The International Protection Bill 2026 delivers on the Programme for Government commitment to implement the new EU Migration and Asylum Pact by 12 June 2026. This Bill represents the most significant reform of Irish asylum laws in the history of the State. It will put in place a new framework to manage migration and asylum for the long term. It will improve decision-making structures within the international protection system and provide faster timelines for the processing of international protection applications. The overall objective of the Bill is to provide a fair, sustainable and efficient asylum procedure that is consistent with how asylum laws operate across the EU. The Bill will provide for the timeframes for the different procedures under which an international protection application can be examined, in accordance with the 2024 Asylum Procedures Regulation (APR) and the 2024 Asylum and Migration Management Regulation (AMMR). These timeframes will be 6 months for standard procedures, 3 months for the accelerated procedure, and 2 months for the admissibility procedure. Section 115 of the International Protection Bill sets out the grounds under which the examination of an international protection application can be accelerated. These include cases: • Where the applicant has raised issues that are not relevant to the examination for international protection; • Where the applicant has made inconsistent, contradictory or false representations; • Where the applicant has intentionally misled the authorities by presenting false information or documents or by withholding relevant information or documents, particularly with respect to his or her identity or nationality; • Where the application was made merely to delay or frustrate the enforcement of a return decision; • Where the applicant comes from a safe third country; • Where the applicant is considered to pose a danger to national security or public order; • Where the applicant made a subsequent application; • Where the applicant has entered the State lawfully and, without good reason, has not made an application for international protection as soon as possible; and • Where the applicant comes from a country with a recognition rate across the EU of 20% or less. The Asylum Border Procedure will have a 12-week time limit for first instance and appeal decisions to be completed for applicants from countries of origin with a recognition rate of 20% or less across the EU, or for those who intentionally mislead the authorities by presenting false information or documents or by withholding relevant information or documents, or are deemed a security risk. It is important to note that the grounds in the Bill for application of the Asylum Border Procedure and the accelerated examination procedure are those which are contained in the Asylum Procedures Regulation, the measure of the EU Pact that governs procedural matters. This is directly applicable in the State and the Bill provides for further and more detailed provisions for the implementation of these measures. It is a feature of the Common European Asylum System, in which Ireland is participating, that the asylum process should be standardised across EU Member States. I am satisfied that the categories provided for the application of the Asylum Border Procedure and the accelerated examination procedure are sufficient for Ireland’s needs in terms of a fair, sustainable, and efficient asylum procedure.

question: 342. Deputy Carol Nolan asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the way In which the extension of the reckonable residence requirement to five years for citizenship applications by those granted international protection under the International Protection Bill 2026 will deter non-genuine claims and support sustainable integration limits; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [7121/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration Last November I secured Government approval to introduce new policies and legislative changes to strengthen Ireland’s migration and asylum system to ensure it is rules-based, efficient and more aligned with EU Member States. As part of this, a number of changes are planned to the rules on the granting of Irish citizenship. One such policy change relates to the residency requirements of a person granted refugee status and who wishes to apply for Irish citizenship. This change came into effect on 8 December 2025. Previously, individuals granted international protection status could apply for citizenship after a period of three years. Effective from 8 December 2025 refugees are generally required to have five years of reckonable residence in the State to meet the eligibility criteria for citizenship. The extension of the reckonable residence requirement reinforces the principle that Irish citizenship reflects a sustained and meaningful connection with the State, demonstrated over time. This approach is especially important in the context of the International Protection Bill which will see accelerated procedure times in the processing of international protection applications, while maintaining an appropriate period of residence prior to eligibility for citizenship. In addition, the requirement supports sustainable integration outcomes by providing a longer period during which those with international protection status can establish themselves in Irish society, including through participation in employment, education and community life, prior to applying for citizenship. Applications for citizenship submitted prior to 8 December 2025 will continue to be assessed in accordance with the previous residency requirement, while applications submitted on and after that date are assessed under the revised policy. All applications for a certificate of naturalisation are assessed individually based on the provisions of the Irish Nationality and Citizenship Act 1956, as amended. Applications are assessed in line with the policy and legislative framework in force at the time the application is made. I want to clarify that International Protection applicants are not eligible to apply for naturalisation. Only individuals who have been granted an International Protection declaration and who have accrued the required period of reckonable residence in the State can be considered for Irish citizenship. There has been no change in this regard. The recent policy change relates solely to the length of reckonable residence required.

question: 343. Deputy Malcolm Byrne asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the way in which his Department ensures that there is consistency in decision making in applications for asylum in Ireland. [7163/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 343 and 344 together. The complex nature of the International Protection system requires in-depth training and the International Protection Office (IPO) works closely with the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) in developing and delivering this training to its staff and panel members. A comprehensive training programme is in place for all IPO caseworkers and panel members involved in interviewing applicants and considering international protection applications. The training sets out the international, European and national context of protection and the legal framework within which the office works. This is delivered in conjunction with the with UNHCR Dublin office. The training includes the subjects listed below: • An introduction to International Protection • International, European & national context • The legal framework in place in Ireland • An overview of the IPO • Role of panel members • Intercultural awareness • Overview of refugee and subsidiary protection definitions and credibility analysis • Considering nationality, statelessness & article 1E of the 1951 Refugee Convention • Assessments of facts and circumstances including credibility, well founded fear, objective basis and persecution • Convention grounds – race, religion, nationality, membership of a particular social group, political opinion • Subsidiary protection – serious harm • Permission to remain • State protection • Internal protection alternative • Exclusion clauses • Interviewing techniques • Specific claims relating to vulnerable applicants, children, victims of Sexual and Gender-Based Violence (SGBV), Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity (SOGI) • Human Trafficking • Interviewing vulnerable applicants • Administrative law & judicial review • Working with interpreters • Data protection • Interview set up/practicalities • Report template and practice note • Case management and style guide • Country of Origin Information (COI) and its use • Case study exercise International Protection Officers can only make recommendations on applicant cases having fully completed the above training and having undergone required mentoring with the IPO case processing unit. IPO case officers use country of origin information as a core element of the decision-making process in international protection applications. COI is embedded in officer induction training, where new officers are trained on sourcing, assessing, and applying COI appropriately in credibility and risk assessment. This is further reinforced through European Union Agency for Asylum (EUAA) training modules undertaken by IPO officers, in particular: • EUAA COI training modules (including COI methodology and practical application) • Evidence assessment • Asylum interview method (including specialist modules on vulnerable applicants and children) Together, these ensure that IPO decision-makers are consistently trained in the effective and objective use of COI in line with EU and international best practice.

question: 346. Deputy Roderic O'Gorman asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration for an update on the establishment of the Fingal West Community Safety Partnership; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [7223/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration The Policing, Security and Community Safety Act 2024, which I commenced on 2 April last, provides for the establishment of Local Community Safety Partnerships (LCSP) within each local authority area. A number of administrative steps need to be undertaken to facilitate the establishment of a Safety Partnership in a given area, including nomination of proposed members by local authorities and statutory bodies, and the appointment of all members by myself as Minister. On 11 December 2026, I appointed members to Fingal West Local Community Safety Partnerships. The convening of meetings is a matter determined at local level. That being said, I am informed that the inaugural meeting of Fingal West Safety Partnership was held on Wednesday 28 January 2026 at which they elected their Chair, Phillip Jennings and Vice Chair Councillor John Walsh. The regulations for the Safety Partnerships came into operation on Monday 30 June, and a total of 36 Partnerships are in the process of being established in local authority areas across the country. The National Office for Community Safety, an office of my Department, is providing support to local authorities and in particular to Local Community Safety Partnership teams, in the process of establishing each Safety Partnership in their area.

question: 347. Deputy Seán Ó Fearghaíl asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration if he will consider important issues relating to the Irish Prison Service, raised in correspondence (details supplied); and if he will make a statement on the matter. [7231/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration The Deputy will appreciate that the issues raised are operational matters for the Irish Prison Service (IPS) and as Minister I cannot comment on any individual cases the Deputy refers to. I am aware of correspondence on the matter and I am advised that the IPS are communicating directly with the individual concerned in relation to the issues raised.

question: 348. Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the total expenditure incurred by the State on accommodation and related supports for international protection applicants in each of the years from 2022 to 2025 to date; the projected total expenditure for 2026; and to provide a breakdown of this expenditure under the following headings: payments to private accommodation providers, expenditure on State-owned accommodation, ancillary service costs, and administrative costs; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [7240/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration Providing reception conditions to people who are applying for international protection is part of EU and Irish law. The State is currently accommodating over 33,000 people seeking international protection in over 312 International Protection Accommodation Service (IPAS) centres around the country. Ireland has adopted and is now working to implement the EU Pact on Migration and Asylum in mid-2026. Reforming and speeding up processing of applications should also serve over time to reduce the scale of the demand for international protection accommodation. The Department is working to increase the amount of State-owned international protection accommodation and creating a more stable and sustainable accommodation system. As developing these more sustainable state-owned accommodation system options will take time, the commissioning of emergency commercial accommodation will continue to be a feature in the short to medium term. The allocation for IPAS accommodation and supports for 2025 was €1.27 billion and this has reduced to €1.1 billion for accommodation and supports in 2026. Please see, in tabular format, the total spend on IPAS accommodation in commercial and State-owned accommodation since 2022. Please note the 2025 figure is provisional pending completion of the 2025 Appropriation Accounts. 2022 €356,554,000 2023 €651,756,000 2024 €1.005 billion 2025 €1.2 billion The costs outlined below pertain to accommodation for international protection applicants, including transport, facilities management, utilities and other related costs. The breakdown of data requested with respect to payments to private accommodation providers, expenditure on State-owned accommodation, ancillary service costs, and administrative costs is not collated or readily available. The Department is also taking action across all aspects of the accommodation system to improve value for money, and to strengthen governance, compliance, and integration supports. A range of updated systems and procedures have been put in place and are already having an impact. IPAS has put improved processes in place for appraisal, validation, contracting and payments. The introduction of a new rate card model is driving costs down for new and renewed contracts, and I am pleased to note this has already saved approximately €77 million in 2025. This reform within the accommodation system has laid the basis for continued process improvement and costs savings in 2026. There is full transparency from the Department in terms of providers receiving payments, with details of all payments over €20,000 and the recipients published quarterly online at: www.gov.ie/en/collection/dfdadb-department-of-children-and-youth-affairs-purchase-orders-for-20000-o/

question: 349. Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the total number of international protection applicants accommodated by the State at the end of each quarter from Quarter 1 2023 to Quarter 4 2025; the number currently awaiting an accommodation offer; the average duration of stay in State-provided accommodation during this period; and the measures in place to reduce both length of stay and associated costs; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [7241/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration Providing reception conditions – accommodation and other basic supports – to people seeking international protection is part of Irish and EU law. The length of time a person is entitled to access IPAS accommodation is directly related to the duration of their application for international protection. Ireland has adopted and is now working to implement the EU Pact on Migration and Asylum in mid-2026. Reforming and speeding up processing of applications, which is well underway, should reduce the scale of the demand for international protection accommodation, and the time each applicant spends in IPAS accommodation. The State is currently accommodating over 33,000 people who have applied for international protection in Ireland, and over 9,700 of these residents are children. Below is a table outlining the number of people accommodated by the International Protection Accommodation Service (IPAS), per quarter for 2023-2025. - Q1 Q2 Q3 Q4 2023 20,307 21,573 23,983 26,279 2024 28,478 31,375 32,378 32,774 2025 33,025 32,770 32,636 33,241 The average length of stay in IPAS Accommodation across all 312 centres and all residents is currently 24.8 months. Not all international protection applicants are resident in IPAS accommodation and the length of time spent by a person resident in IPAS accommodation will vary depending on the individual circumstances of the person or family's application. Extensive challenges were posed to the State in sourcing international protection accommodation during an unprecedented surge in applications from 2022 to 2024. Many of the impacts of this surge period remain in place at this time, though significant change is underway. During this period, over 45,000 additional international protection applicants arrived in Ireland. Prior to this, a typical 3-year period would have seen close to 8,000 or 9,000 arrivals. This increase in applications placed intense pressure on accommodation supply, and also on application processing and the timelines associated. As such, efforts to reduce the length of stay in IPAS are focused on reducing processing times for international protection applications. As a result of accommodation shortages and the need to prioritise accommodation for people who are most vulnerable, IPAS cannot make offers of accommodation to all single male applicants on arrival. The number of people awaiting an offer of accommodation from IPAS is currently 453, reduced from a high of 3,500 in March of 2025. In relation to costs of IPAS accommodation, as well as reducing processing times, there is an ongoing move toward providing more State-owned accommodation, which represents better value for money than commercial provision. The State purchase of Citywest in 2025 was an important milestone in this regard. While commercial provision will be needed to meet demand in the medium term, the Department is reviewing and renegotiating all contracts as they expire, applying a new rate card pricing model that has already delivered approximately €77m in savings since May 2025. Along with other measures to increase inspections and compliance, and ending non-performing contracts, greater control and value for money is being exerted over the IPAS system. While commissioning emergency commercial accommodation will continue to be necessary in the short to medium term, it is being contracted on a short-term basis, which will enable the State to decommission this capacity with agility as contracts expire or demand fluctuates.

question: 350. Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration whether his Department has carried out any value-for-money assessments, cost-benefit analyses, or benchmarking exercises in respect of contracts entered into with private accommodation providers for international protection applicants since 2022; to detail the findings of any such assessments; and to outline the steps taken to renegotiate, terminate, or replace high-cost contracts; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [7242/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 350 and 352 together. The Department is taking action across all aspects of the international protection accommodation system, in line with Government policy and the Programme for Government. These actions include a move toward greater State-owned provision, improving value for money, and strengthening governance, compliance, and integration supports. Following unprecedented increases in applications for international protection from 2022 to 2024, a crisis response was required from the State to source accommodation at pace, and under pressure. Much of the accommodation now in use within the IPAS system was sourced during this period and under these circumstances, at the same time as the State was responding to accommodation needs of a huge number of people fleeing the war in Ukraine, amid ongoing pressures in the housing market. Applications for international protection have reduced during 2025, though they remain high compared to pre-2022 levels. This reduction has allowed department officials to put in place greater controls over the IPAS accommodation portfolio after the unprecedented increase in arrivals in recent years, which necessitated a crisis response to source accommodation. A range of updated systems and procedures have been put in place and are already having an impact. IPAS has put improved processes in place for appraisal, validation, contracting and payments. This reform within the accommodation system has laid the basis for continued process improvement and costs savings in 2026. The introduction of a new rate card model is driving costs down for new and renewed contracts, and I am pleased to note this has already saved approximately €77 million across 134 new or renewed contracts in 2025. The rate card is considered commercially sensitive as it is used in live negotiations, but it functions as a bench-mark rate across various types of accommodation, and is being used to renegotiate rates and define rates for any new contracts. Inspections and compliance reviews have also increased since 2024, and 22 contracts were ended in 2026. In contracting accommodation over recent years, despite significant pressures on accommodation supply, the Department has worked to avoid competing with the residential property market, and in the current process, properties which are designated as residential properties are not considered suitable for appraisal by the Department as offers of international protection accommodation. The Department is developing more State-owned accommodation from a range of sources, including using State-owned sites for temporary accommodation. State-owned accommodation offers significantly improved value for money compared to commercial accommodation in this sector. A key milestone was the State's purchase of Citywest in 2025, which has increased the overall State-owned bed numbers from 900 spaces in 2024 to over 4,000 today. Developing more State-owned options will allow us to move away from the current degree of reliance on commercial provision. While commissioning emergency commercial accommodation will continue to be necessary in the short to medium term, it is being contracted on a short-term basis, which will enable the State to decommission this capacity with agility as contracts expire or demand fluctuates. An overall reform of the international protection system is underway that is already working to speed up the processing of applications and should reduce the need for constant growth in the accommodation system, such as was experienced in recent years.

question: 351. Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration to outline the policy rationale, projected fiscal impact, and anticipated savings associated with proposals to require international protection applicants who are in employment to make a contribution towards the cost of their accommodation; the estimated annual savings arising from this measure; the safeguards envisaged to ensure proportionality and compliance; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [7243/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration The 2025 Programme for Government includes a commitment to introducing a contribution model for people in international protection accommodation. Proposals for residents to make a contribution to the cost of international protection accommodation were considered by Government and are now being progressed by the Department. The contribution to cost scheme will be implemented within a planned 12-month period, allowing for the development of systems and resources to assess eligibility, share data securely and collect and process payments. IPAS Accommodation is provided for in EU regulations and transposed into Irish law. Statutory Instrument No 230/2018, European Communities (Reception Conditions) Regulations 2018, provides that all IP applicants are entitled to Material Reception Conditions. This is defined as housing, food and associated benefits provided in kind, the daily expenses allowance (DEA), and clothing provided by way of financial allowance under section 201 of the Social Welfare Consolidation Act 2005. DEA is currently set at €38.80 per week per adult and €29.80 per week per child. Because of the specific legal status of people applying to for international protection, during their application process they do not have access to standard social welfare benefits, nor to standard housing services and entitlements. As such, any State accommodation which is provided to them as part of material reception conditions is not private rented accommodation and is subject to the above regulations instead. The Regulations further provide, at section 5, that where a resident is in receipt of an income above a certain level, they may be required to make a contribution to the cost of providing reception condition services. The implementation process, which is underway, will include procurement of an appropriate third-party provider service, and this procurement process will involve further detailed analysis as the scheme comes into operation. The contribution rates are set out in a Schedule to the Regulations and are proportionate to the amount that people earn, as set out below. Weekly Income € Potential Contribution € % of weekly income €97.01 - €150 €15 15.5 -10% €150.01 - €210 €35.70 23.8 – 17% €210.01 - €275 €59.50 28.3 - 21.6% €275.01 - €340 €83.30 30.3 - 24.5% €340.01 - €405 €119 35 - 29.4% €405.01 - €470 €154.70 38.2 – 33% €470.01 - €535 €178.50 38 – 33% €535.01 - €600 €202.30 38 – 34% €600.01 + €238 39.60% The introduction of this contribution for international protection applicants who are working and earning and income is aligned with processes already in place in other EU member states. The scheme will have a review and appeals process incorporated into the process as it is developed for implementation. Further information on the scheme will be made available as implementation progresses during 2026.

question: 353. Deputy Barry Ward asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration if his attention has been drawn to a report (details supplied) in relation to the welfare of persons in Irish prisons; the actions he will take to address the issues highlighted in the report; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [7248/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 354 and 353 together. I am aware that the Irish Prison Service (IPS) published the fifth and sixth annual Self-Harm Assessment and Data Analysis (SADA) Reports on Monday 26 January 2026. These reports provide a comprehensive overview of self-harm incidents across the prison estate during the 2022 to 2024 reporting periods. The reports provide important insights into the complex factors associated with self-harm in custody, including mental ill-health, addiction, trauma, and stressors linked to imprisonment. Information is also included on trends associated with types of self harm and periods when self harm seems to be more prevalent. The IPS's partnership with the HSE, the National Suicide Research Foundation, and the Samaritans remains central to ensuring that people in custody receive timely, compassionate support. Every incident of self harm represents a person in distress, and the IPS remains fully committed to creating safer, more supportive environments across the prison estate. Across both reporting periods, the findings highlight the need for continued investment in trauma-informed, multidisciplinary approaches. I am advised that the IPS continues to prioritise suicide and self-harm prevention through psychology and in-reach psychiatric services, enhanced staff training, improved information-sharing and early identification of risk, an updated standard operating procedure in relation to Safety Observation Cells, the Samaritans Listener Scheme, and strengthened collaboration with the HSE and community-based services. The IPS is also working to strengthen its committal health assessments, and provide targeted supports for individuals who engage in self harm. The collaborative efforts of the SADA project guides the IPS in creating a safer environment for all people in custody. The findings continue to inform the development of self-harm prevention strategies within the IPS, aligned with broader justice and health objectives.

question: 356. Deputy Barry Ward asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration if his attention has been drawn to the case of a prisoner (details supplied); the actions he will take to ensure that this person is provided a suitable diet to accommodate their diagnosed medical condition; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [7301/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 357, 356, 358 and 359 together. The Irish Prison Service Catering Service provides a nutritionally balanced, varied diet to all prisoners through the 28 day menu. This menu meets the requirements of the majority of prisoners' dietary requirements, including people who are diabetic. It also caters for special dietary needs as required. For example, diabetics may request additional fruit. Provisions are made for particular requirements of different religions, for example people from the Muslim faith who require a Halal diet, people from the Jewish faith who require a Kosher diet, and people from the Hindu faith who are strictly vegetarian. The IPS also ensures that food is stored, prepared and served appropriately, provision is also made for religious abstinence from certain foods or food processes. Requests for the accommodation of specific dietary requirements and/or restrictions, including those related to medical conditions are referred to the prison doctor for approval. Each request is managed on a case-by-case basis.

question: 360. Deputy Eoin Ó Broin asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number of first residence permits issued in each of the years from 2016 to 2024 that were for education; and the number of residence permits for education valid in each of years from 2016 to 2024. [7306/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration The Programme for Government contains a commitment to publish a National Migration and Integration Strategy detailing how the Government intends to meet the demands and opportunities facing Ireland’s society and economy over the next decade. My Department is currently working with other colleagues in Government Departments to develop this strategy with the aim to publish it later this year. As part of this strategic approach, I am reviewing the area of student permissions, including with regard to English Language students. This work is aimed at ensuring that the system remains robust and rules-based, supports high-quality education providers, and continues to offer a positive experience for genuine students coming to Ireland. International students from outside the EU/EEA are granted a residence permission on Stamp 2 conditions where they have enrolled on, and commenced a course listed on the Interim List of Eligible Programmes (ILEP), or eligible programmes offered by providers with authorisation to use the new TrustEd Education mark awarded by the Quality and Qualifications Ireland (QQI). I understand the Deputy has agreed to limit the scope of his request to data from 2018 onwards. The table below lists the number of Stamp 2 student residence permissions issued by my Department from 2018 to 2025. Year Stamp 2 residence permissions issued 2018 44,464 2019 49,658 2020 30,980 2021 28,717 2022 52,845 2023 60,882 2024 60,901 2025** 56,512 *Please note, figures are correct at time of issue, however, all statistics may be subject to data cleansing. **Statistics for 2025 are impacted by delays to registration due to current overall pressure on this function; the final figure for those required to register Stamp 2 permissions will exceed that set out in the table. I can inform the Deputy that the figures provided account for the number of people, or unique individuals, required to register or renew their immigration permission in a calendar year, it is not possible to provide the number of these people who registered for the first time or who renewed their permission more than once in each given year without examining thousands of individual files. question: 361. Deputy Matt Carthy asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number of EU citizens subject to re-entry bans to the State in each of the past ten years; the average duration of the bans imposed in each year, in tabular form; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [7321/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 361 and 364 together. Under the European Communities (Free Movement of Persons) Regulations 2015, which transposes the Free Movement Directive (Directive 2004/38/EC) into Irish law, orders can be made for both the removal and exclusion of citizens of the European Union, European Economic Area and Switzerland. Such orders can be made on the grounds of public policy, public security or public health; legally, such orders must not be disproportionate and an individual assessment of factors such as length of residence in the country, integration (e.g. work history), age, health etc. must be carried out. These orders, and their legal basis, are distinct from deportation orders which are legal orders to leave the State and apply in respect of non-EEA nationals only. I can advise the Deputy that on Sunday 25 January 2026, removal orders were enforced against 17 Polish citizens and 16 Lithuanian citizens who were removed from Ireland by charter flight. This was the State's second ever charter EU removal flight following an operation in October 2025 to remove 23 Romanian citizens. These removal orders were made in accordance with the Free Movement Directive on grounds of criminality and re-entry bans of up to 10 years have been applied to prevent return to Ireland. I understand the Deputy has agreed to limit the scope of his request to data from 2020 onwards. The table below details the number of removal orders which have been enforced under the European Communities (Free Movement of Persons) Regulations 2015 between 2020 and 2025, and the average duration of enforced exclusion orders. Year Orders signed under the Directive Orders enforced Average period of Exclusion Order 2020 33 32 4.7 years 2021 40 42 5.3 years 2022 58 37 4.6 years 2023 19 21 3.7 years 2024 24 18 3.4 years 2025 157 56 3.85 years 2026 (to 28 January) 11 35 5.6 years * Please note, figures are correct at time of issue, however, all statistics may be subject to data cleansing. Removal Orders enforced in any given year may have been made in prior years. There may be a time lag between the making of a Removal Order and its enforcement in circumstances such as where the subject is continuing to serve a period of imprisonment. When issued with such an order, the person concerned is required to remove themselves from the State. Many people comply with this and leave the country without informing my Department; as such it is not always possible to record these departures definitively. The costs for the provision of the aircraft for the charter removal flight to Romania in October 2025 was €69,475 (ex. VAT). For the charter removal flight to Poland and Lithuania on 25 January, the cost was €122,660 (ex. VAT) for a return flight. A breakdown of commercial flight costs for EU removals is not available at this time, but I will write to the Deputy when this is available.

question: 362. Deputy Barry Ward asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration if his attention has been drawn to the concerns of an organisation (details supplied), in relation to the use of counselling notes as set out in the Criminal Law and Civil Law (Miscellaneous Provisions) Bill 2025; the actions he will take to address these concerns; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [7329/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 362 and 363 together. This Government is committed to ensuring that legislative provisions balance victims' constitutional rights to personal privacy, the important role of counselling in their recovery, but also the accused person’s constitutional right to a fair trial. Robust protections must be applied to the handling of victims’ counselling notes in the context of criminal trials. There have been calls for a complete ban on counselling notes, however, the Attorney General’s Office has advised that a blanket ban on the disclosure of counselling records is not compatible with the Constitution. It is in this context that I am bringing forward legislation to require that a disclosure hearing takes place in all cases, removing the provision that allows for this vital judicial oversight to be waived. I am committed to restricting intrusions into victims’ privacy rights, to the maximum extent possible. The Criminal Law and Civil Law (Miscellaneous Provisions) Bill 2026 was debated at Second stage in Dáil Éireann on 22 January. This legislation amends the current statutory framework to ensure that judicial oversight governs the disclosure of any counselling records. From now on, if counselling records are sought by the defence, a judge will scrutinise the material and make an impartial and objective decision on whether disclosure is necessary in the interests of justice. I also intend to bring further legislative amendments by way of Committee stage amendments to the Criminal Law and Civil Law (Miscellaneous Provisions) Bill 2026 to restrict the disclosure of counselling records to the maximum extent possible. In particular, I will introduce a presumption of non-disclosure in respect of counselling notes, meaning the default position will be that counselling notes are not to be disclosed, save for the very small number of cases where disclosure is warranted in the interest of justice. In addition, I am seeking to ensure that the same protection regime is applied to other victims’ records containing sensitive personal data, such as medical records, child protection records and other such documents. Overall, these reforms will mean that proposed disclosure of any sensitive personal material will only occur where this is absolutely necessary, while any such disclosure will be subject to impartial and objective judicial scrutiny. Insofar as legal aid is concerned, additional resources have been provided to the Legal Aid Board for 2026 and it is my expectation that this increased funding will ensure that the Board can support victims in the criminal justice process. Officials in my Department met with the organisation referred to by the Deputy earlier this month and we will continue this engagement going forward.

question: 100. Deputy Barry Ward asked the Minister for Social Protection the number of persons currently in receipt of financial support under the international protection system; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [6945/26]
answer: Minister for Social Protection My department administers the Daily Expenses Allowance which is paid to International Protection Applicants who reside in, or are waiting for, accommodation provided by the International Protection Accommodation Services. The current weekly Daily Expense Allowance rates of payment are €38.80 per adult and €29.80 per child. In December 2023 an increased rate of €113.80 per week for an adult was introduced where a person is unaccommodated and is on a waiting list for accommodation with the International Protection Accommodation Services. question: 120. Deputy Martin Daly asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the way the current court fees regime (S.I. No. 492 of 2014) aligns with the State’s obligation to ensure effective access to the courts for the protection and vindication of constitutional rights; if he will introduce an explicit exemption from High Court stamp fees for proceedings brought primarily to vindicate fundamental rights; and the timeframe in which he plans to bring forward any amending statutory instrument. [6696/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 120 and 121 together. Matters in regard to court fees are set by Statutory Instrument made by the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration, with the consent of the Minister for Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation. The court fee structures currently in place are designed to be proportionate and balanced to ensure continued access to justice, while supporting appropriate contribution to the efficient running of the court system overall. The current fees system reflects the need to ensure the interests of applicants, as well as considering the public interest in the smooth operation of the court system. This balance of interests, as well as applicable administrative considerations, is evident in the extensive range of existing exemptions from court fees already in place, in regard to specific categories of proceedings and by some State bodies. Matters arising in relation to court fees are kept under consideration by my Department, as appropriate. I can confirm that S.I. No. 492/2014 (Supreme Court, Court of Appeal and High Court (Fees) Order 2014) is currently under review with a view to revising a number of its provisions to resolve an issue which has arisen as a result of a recent High Court judgement regarding the exemption for habeas corpus actions and to provide for an exemption for Qualified Entities under the Representative Actions for the Protection of the Collective Interests of Consumers Act 2023. It should also be noted that in accordance with, and subject to, Part 11 of the Legal Services Regulation Act 2015, parties who are entirely successful in civil proceedings are entitled to their costs.

question: 122. Deputy Ciarán Ahern asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration if he will consider exercising his discretionary powers to grant leave to remain to an asylum applicant (details supplied) on humanitarian grounds; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [6748/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration As the Deputy may be aware, my Department is unable to publish any information that would identify any person as being an international protection applicant. This is a separate matter to the law dealing with data protection matters more generally. My officials and I are legally obliged, under Section 26 of the International Protection Act 2015, to ensure that the identity of any person who applies for international protection is kept confidential. Section 26(1) sets out that: “the Minister and the Tribunal and their respective officers shall take all practicable steps to ensure that the identity of applicants is kept confidential”. As I am sure you will appreciate, these confidentiality requirements are especially important for an asylum-seeker, whose claim inherently supposes a fear of persecution by the authorities of their home country and whose situation, or that of their family or friends still living in the country from which they have sought protection, can be jeopardised if the protection of their personal information is not ensured. An applicant for such protection status, or their legal representative, should contact either the International Protection Office (IPO) or the International Protection Appeals Tribunal (IPAT) directly, as appropriate if they wish to receive an update on the status of their case. Contact information for The International Protection Office can be found at: https://www.ipo.gov.ie/en/ipo/pages/contactus. Contact information for The International Protection Appeals Tribunal can be found at: www.protectionappeals.ie/contact-us/. Both the International Protection Office (IPO) and the International Protection Appeals Tribunal (IPAT) are fully independent in deciding whether or not to grant international protection. Each application is examined individually on its own merits, in line with national and international asylum law. They are also bound by confidentiality provisions in respect of applicants as set out in the International Protection 2015 Act.
